title: Recognising Regional Terroir
quiz.0.question: In blind tasting, which combination of features best points to northern Italy (Piedmont/Trentino)?
quiz.0.options.0: Low acid + full body + black fruit
quiz.0.options.1: High acid + fine tannins + minerality + red fruit
quiz.0.options.2: Low tannin + tropical fruit + high alcohol
quiz.0.options.3: Medium acid + creamy oak + no minerality
quiz.0.explanation: The cool climate of the North (especially Piedmont and Trentino) gives high acidity, fine tannins, minerality and red-fruit aromas — a sharp contrast with the low acid and high alcohol of the South.
quiz.1.question: What is the most recognisable terroir feature of Tuscany (Chianti Classico/Brunello) in blind tasting?
quiz.1.options.1: Sour cherry + dried herbs + Tuscan earthiness
quiz.1.options.3: Lots of oaky vanilla + high residual sugar
quiz.1.explanation: Tuscany is dominated by Sangiovese; sour cherry + dried herbs (rosemary, thyme) + the dusty tannic texture from Tuscany's reddish-brown soils (galestro/alberese) are its most recognisable terroir features.
quiz.2.question: Which Italian area's whites are most typically marked by a "bitter-almond finish + minerality" from volcanic tuff soils?
quiz.2.explanation: Campania's Greco di Tufo and Fiano di Avellino grow on volcanic tuff, which brings a distinctive minerality + bitter-almond finish — the most terroir-recognisable feature of southern Italian whites.
quiz.3.question: When recognising Piemonte's terroir, which aromas are the key identifier of the Langhe (Barolo/Barbaresco)?
quiz.3.options.1: Tar + rose + dried leaves (the Nebbiolo trio)
quiz.3.explanation: Nebbiolo's terroir identifier in the Langhe (Barolo/Barbaresco) is the trio "tar + rose (when young) → dried leaves/mushroom (with age)", supported by high acidity and fine tannins.
slides.0.title: Recognising Regional Terroir
slides.0.subtitle: From north-south differences to microclimates: identifying Italian regions blind
slides.1.title: North vs South Terroir in Italy: The First Filter in Blind Tasting
slides.1.content:
From the Alps to the Mediterranean, Italy stretches over 1,000 km from north to south, with marked climatic differences. In blind tasting, first narrow the field with a "north or south" judgement, then identify the specific area.

🏔️ The North (cool climate)

Piedmont / Trentino / Alto Adige / Friuli

High acidity | fine tannins | strong minerality | mainly red fruit | long ageing potential

🌿 The Centre (temperate climate)

Tuscany / Umbria / Marche / Lazio

Medium-high acidity | medium tannins + dusty texture | dried-herb aromas | red and black fruit together | earthy minerality

☀️ The South (warm climate)

Campania / Puglia / Basilicata / Calabria

Lower acidity | high alcohol (14%+) | black fruit + spice | volcanic/mineral notes (Campania)

🌋 The Islands (extreme climate)

Sicily / Sardinia

Intense sunshine | low acid, high alcohol (Nero d'Avola) | but high-altitude volcanic Etna is the exception (high acid)
slides.2.title: Recognising the Terroir of Three Northern Areas
slides.2.content:
Piedmont / Alto Adige / Friuli — three quite different northern styles

🍷 Piedmont (the Langhe hills)
Soils: Tortonian clay-marl (La Morra) + Serravallian calcareous marl and sandstone (Serralunga)
Terroir signatures: Nebbiolo — rose + tar + liquorice | Barbera — high acid, low tannin, crisp
Clues: high acid + complex structure + minerality; Nebbiolo is the most recognisable
🏔️ Alto Adige / Trentino (Alpine)
Soils: porphyry, dolomitic limestone, schist, glacial moraine (200-1000 m)
Terroir signatures: Pinot Grigio — crisp minerality | Riesling — high acid, floral | Gewürztraminer — lychee and rose
Clues: very high acidity + clean, cool minerality + clear varietal aromas, unlike any other Italian area
🌊 Friuli Venezia Giulia
Soils: ponca (marl and sandstone), the Collio hills
Terroir signatures: Friulano — almond finish + white flowers | Ribolla Gialla — high acid, crisp
Clues: orange wine (skin-contact white) is Friuli's special style, with oxidative notes + tannic texture
slides.3.title: Recognising Terroir Differences Within Tuscany
slides.3.content:
Tuscany centres on Sangiovese, but different areas' terroirs bring marked style differences that can be recognised blind.

Chianti Classico

  • Soils: galestro (friable, flaky marl) + alberese (hard limestone)
  • Acidity: high (pH 3.3-3.6)
  • Aromas: sour cherry + dried herbs + earthiness
  • Tannins: medium + dusty texture (from galestro)
  • Recognition: Gran Selezione has more elegant florals and finer tannins

Brunello di Montalcino

  • Soils: varied (sandstone, clay, limestone, volcanic)
  • Acidity: high (pH 3.3-3.5)
  • Aromas: sour cherry + rose + minerality (more complex than Chianti)
  • Tannins: more powerful and firmer than Chianti
  • Recognition: richer fruit + a longer finish
slides.4.title: Recognising the Special Terroirs of the South and the Islands
slides.4.content:
🌋 Campania (volcanic soils)

Taurasi DOCG / Greco di Tufo / Fiano di Avellino

Volcanic tuff brings a distinctive minerality | Aglianico: black fruit + smoky volcanic ash | whites: honey + roasted hazelnut + minerality

☀️ Puglia (sunny plains)

Primitivo / Negroamaro / Salice Salentino

Italy's warmest, flattest area | blackberry jam + chocolate + high alcohol (14-16%) | low acid + full body | the most typical southern style

🌋 Etna (Sicily's volcano)

Nerello Mascalese (high-altitude volcano)

High altitude (600-1000 m) overturns the image of Sicily | high acid + fine tannins + volcanic minerality | often mistaken for Burgundy Pinot Noir

🏝️ Sardinia (Mediterranean island)

Cannonau (Grenache) / Vermentino

Cannonau: ripe fruit + spice + medium acidity | Vermentino: a white with citrus + fennel + savoury, saline minerality
slides.5.title: Key Takeaways
slides.5.points.0: A north-south judgement is the first filter in blind tasting: the North is high in acid and mineral; the Centre medium-high acid with dried herbs; the South low in acid and high in alcohol
slides.5.points.1: Piedmont's terroir signatures: Nebbiolo's rose and tar + complex structure; Barbera's crisp high acid and low tannin
slides.5.points.2: Alto Adige traits: very high acidity + clean, cool minerality, clear varietal aromas — Italy's style closest to Germany/Austria
slides.5.points.3: Chianti Classico vs Brunello: Brunello is richer and more complex, with a longer finish and firmer tannins
slides.5.points.4: Recognising Campania's volcanic soils: whites with honey, hazelnut and minerality; Aglianico with black fruit, smoke and volcanic ash
slides.5.points.5: Etna (high-altitude Sicilian volcano): high acid, fine tannins, minerality, often mistaken for Burgundy Pinot Noir
slides.5.points.6: Recognising Puglia: Italy's warmest area, low acid and high alcohol (14-16%), blackberry jam and chocolate, the most typical southern style
slides.5.points.7: Friuli orange wine (skin contact): oxidative notes + tannic texture, a special clue when a white wine shows tannin
slides.5.points.8: Geographic reasoning in blind tasting: first confirm north or south, then the climate type, and finally refine grape and area

slides.6.questions.1.question: What is the most recognisable terroir feature of Tuscany (Chianti Classico/Brunello) in blind tasting?
slides.6.questions.1.options.1: Sour cherry + dried herbs + dusty Tuscan earthiness

slides.6.questions.1.explanation: Tuscany is dominated by Sangiovese; sour cherry + dried herbs (rosemary, thyme) + the dusty tannic texture from galestro's flaky marl are the most recognisable Tuscan terroir features.
slides.6.questions.2.question: Which Italian area's whites show a "bitter-almond finish + minerality" because they grow on volcanic tuff?

slides.6.questions.3.question: In blind tasting, which area's wine is Etna's (Sicily's volcano) Nerello Mascalese most often mistaken for?
slides.6.questions.3.explanation: Etna's high-altitude (600-1000 m) volcanic slopes bring high acidity, fine tannins and minerality, and Nerello Mascalese is also fairly pale — features that often lead to it being mistaken for Burgundy Pinot Noir.
slides.6.questions.4.question: What is the key aroma signature for recognising Piemonte's Langhe (Barolo/Barbaresco)?
slides.6.questions.4.options.2: Tropical fruit and chocolate (more like Puglia)
slides.6.questions.4.options.3: Grass and white flowers (more like Alto Adige)
slides.6.questions.4.explanation: Nebbiolo's terroir identifier in the Langhe is the trio "tar + rose (when young) → dried leaves/mushroom (with age)", supported by high acidity and fine tannins — the Langhe's most recognisable combination of terroir features.
